notes: Hand-designed slice arena. Player at the bottom, Brown+Grey+Teal across the top.
The centre pillar sits on the Teal->player line, so Teal must bank a ricochet off a side wall.
The east pillar is the bank-shot reflector: a shell from Teal can clear the centre pillar by going around it, bank off the east pillar's west face, and reach the player beyond.

Cover depth: the centre pillar's lower tier. With the upper tier alone, Brown's and Grey's lines to the player spawn were exactly tangent to its corners -- a knife edge where a 0.1-unit nudge gave one of them a clear 10-unit lane. The lower tier turns that graze into a real chord.

claims.why: The centre pillar's lower tier exists for exactly this: with the upper tier alone, Brown's and Grey's lines to the player spawn were tangent to its corners, and a 0.1-unit nudge opened a clear lane. spawnBlockRobust checks both intact and breached walls; measured to hold under both with the lower tier in place.

notes: Reshaped in the 2026-07-31 balance pass: the bar is a FULL destructible barrier with three solid anchors, so the halves START sealed -- tanks cannot cross and shells cannot pass until someone blasts a hole. Breaching the bar IS the level.
Four enemies against level 1's three.

claims.why: Blowing the bar's inner end opens the UPPER pair's lane -- the trade the level is built around. Fails if a solid outer end went missing or the trade stopped existing.
The mirrored upper lane.
The LOWER pair stays shielded by the bar's solid anchors however much is destroyed.
Mirrored lower lane.

notes: The rocket debut: two Olives (DEFENSIVE_ROCKET, one rocket in flight) flank high behind destructible shields, with a brown-grey-brown trio behind solid cover.

Each flank column (4 and 28) is open floor top-to-bottom EXCEPT the olive's shield, so blasting a shield opens that vertical lane end-to-end, both ways. The shield is the level's trade, one per flank.

The north anchors deny the olives any diagonal into the player half. The browns' spawn lines are shut by a REAL CHORD through the centre pillar -- the pillar's lower tier exists for ARENA_01's reason: with its upper tier alone, a breached centre peek left both brown lines blocked only by a corner tangency.
The centre peek 'x' (rows 18-20) is breachable mid-field cover on the centre axis, not a spawn-line blocker.

claims.why: The olive's shield is the ONLY wall on its flank column: breaching opens the lane end-to-end both ways -- the player can hunt up it, the olive's rockets command it down.
The mirrored flank: one shield per side is the level's trade.
Unlike level 2, breaching opens NO spawn-to-spawn line here: the trade is lanes for mobile tanks, not spawn lines.
Mirrored olive: same rule.
Trio brown: the centre pillar keeps its line shut after the peek is breached.
Trio grey: same pillar.
Trio brown, mirrored.

The centre pillar's lower tier -- the chord-maker -- exists for this: with the upper tier alone, both browns' post-breach blocks were a single-point corner tangency that a 0.1-unit player nudge opened into a full lane. Found by slab math in review. spawnBlockRobust checks both intact and breached walls; measured to hold under both with the chord-maker in place.

notes: The crossfire debut, and the FIRST shipped board that is not 33x27: 45x33, so the extra space is what makes two simultaneous fronts readable instead of merely crowded.

Six enemies in two fronts at ninety degrees to each other. NORTH is the suppressing front -- GREEN, grey, brown across row 4, behind the bar. EAST is the mobile front -- teal, olive, teal down column 40, inside the player's own half, behind the solid east wall.

The green at (10, 4) is the RICOCHET_SNIPER debut, and it is here because it answers the board's own weakness. 284 of the 1359 open cells are seen by no enemy from its spawn -- one broad region, NOT a tidy corner. Green's ricochets reach 275 cells it has no direct line to, and 171 of those are cells no enemy can otherwise see at all: it covers 171 of the 284. It is stationary like a brown, so the north front keeps its character; it simply does not accept the bar as cover. Column 10 and not 13: from column 13 its reach was larger (394 cells) but it could ricochet onto the nudged player spawn once the bar was breached, which this arena's spawnBlockRobust claim forbids. Every figure above except the column-13 one is recomputed by arena-validation.test.ts; the column-13 figure describes a placement no longer in the shipped grid, so it was recomputed once by hand instead (see task-4-report.md) and is not pinned by any test.

The two fronts want opposite cover, and that IS the level. Cell (22, 22) sits in the bar's shadow -- shut to the north, wide open to the teal at (40, 13) shooting along the corridor below the bar. Cell (28, 22), six cells east, is the exact inverse: shut to every east tank by the east wall, open to the grey down the bar's gap at column 25. Breaking one front's line steps you into the other's. Four lane claims pin both cells in both wall phases.

The two walls are deliberately different KINDS of problem. The bar is porous, solid only in alternating segments, and breachable at columns 13 and 31; the east wall is solid throughout except for one corridor gap, and must be FLANKED rather than blown. From the player's half that means the corridor above it or the open rows below its south end; it is open north of the bar too, but the bar cuts that section off from the player's half. Level 2 taught breaching; level 4 says not every wall answers to it.

Blowing the bar at column 31 opens that column top-to-bottom, giving the brown at (31, 4) a line down to row 28 -- alongside the player spawn, never onto it: the spawn's own blockers are the bar's solid anchors, which no breach touches. That is why spawnBlockRobust holds here and all six sightlineAfterBreach claims read false, unlike level 2 where breaching is meant to open spawn lines.
The destructible at (19, 19) is mid-field cover for the player's left-hand approach, not a spawn-line blocker: losing it hands the teal at (40, 13) a line onto (16, 22).

Measured against the shipped levels on the same probe -- open cells (destructibles EXCLUDED, they are walls until destroyed) seen by no enemy from its spawn, walls intact: arena-04 is 284 of 1359 = 20.9%, the tightest of the four levels that existed when this was written, against arena-01 288/774 = 37.2%, arena-02 369/747 = 49.4%, arena-03 248/792 = 31.3%. The intended step up in pressure for the last level -- 'last' meaning at the time; arena-05 (185/1359 = 13.6%) is tighter still, and its own notes explain why. These five numbers are recomputed by arena-validation.test.ts rather than left as unpinned prose.

claims.why: North-west GREEN, the ricochet sniper: the bar's solid cell at column 10 stands on its direct line and no breach touches it. Its BANK paths are checked separately and in two places -- structuralFailures forbids a stationary banker any ricochet onto the spawn with walls intact, and this arena's spawnBlockRobust claim extends that to the breached phase under nudges. Column 10 is where green survives BOTH; column 13 did not.
North-centre grey: blocked by the bar's solid cell at column 22, straight up the player's own column.

North-east brown: blocked by the bar's solid cell at column 28. Breaching column 31 opens the column beside the player, not the spawn itself -- the lane claim below is the other half of that statement.
East teal, high: the east wall at rows 18-20 is solid and stays so.
East olive: the east wall at rows 21-23. The rocket never gets a free line on a respawning player, which with six enemies on the board it must not.
East teal, low: the east wall at rows 24-26.

All six spawn blocks are solid bar cells or solid east wall cells, so unlike level 2 the spawn survives a full breach. Measured 0 of 24 nudge probes open in BOTH wall phases; the claim is what keeps a future edit from turning one of those six blockers destructible without noticing.
CROSSFIRE, half one of four: the north's centre gun cannot touch (22, 22) in either phase -- the bar shadows it.

CROSSFIRE: but the east teal owns that same cell along the corridor below the bar. Cover from the north is exposure to the east. Together with the pair below, this is the level's whole idea, stated so an edit cannot quietly undo it.

CROSSFIRE, the inversion: six cells east, the grey's line is open down COLUMN 25's gap in the bar -- not column 22, which is one of the three solid cells holding the grey off the player spawn. Widening column 22 would open that spawn line; column 25 is already open floor.
CROSSFIRE: and the east teal is shut out by the east wall. (22, 22) and (28, 22) are exact opposites, and stay so through a full breach.

The bar's west breach: column 13 is otherwise clear from row 4 to row 22, so blowing that cell opens a north-south lane into the player's half. NOTE both endpoints are plain floor -- green sits at column 10, not 13 -- so unlike this arena's other lanes nothing pins this one to a live spawn. It measures the destructible at (13, 13), which is the thing worth measuring.
The bar's east breach, and the bigger trade: column 31 is clear top to bottom, so this one opens the full height of the board -- down to row 28, level with the player spawn but not onto it.
Losing the mid-field cover at (19, 19) hands the east teal the player's left-hand approach. The cover is the player's, so this is a cost the PLAYER pays for a stray shot, not a trade they choose.

notes: The fifth campaign level, and the second board at arena-04's 45x33 size: seven enemies, one more than arena-04's six, continuing the 3/4/5/6/7 progression. All five enemy kinds appear -- green, two grey, brown, two teal, one olive -- so the level asks the player to handle every mechanic the campaign has taught (bank shots, mines, breachable cover, rockets, the ricochet sniper) in the same fight rather than teaching a new one.

The bar (rows 12-14) and the north row it shelters (green, grey, brown) are copied UNCHANGED from arena-04. That reuse is deliberate: green (RICOCHET_SNIPER) bounces TWICE -- ricochetCount 2, not the single bounce most banking kinds get -- so its reachable set is far larger than a one-bounce reflector search would suggest (arena-04's own notes measure it at 275 cells by ricochet). A mirrored west flank wall, tried first for a three-front pincer, opened a ricochet path onto the nudged player spawn once the bar breaches, in three shapes tried (a bare mirror of the east wall including its rows 15-17 gap, the same footprint with that gap closed, and the wall shifted two columns further from green's own column -- the first failed all 4 cardinal nudges, the second failed 2, the third failed all 4 again once filled solid). Everything SOUTH of the bar was redesigned instead, well clear of green's own column and the bar's western gap.

The east flank wall runs the full 15 rows from 18 to 32 -- six rows further south than arena-04's 18-26 -- so it can hold a THIRD spawn at real depth (row 31, one row from the board's own south edge) rather than arena-04's two. It is CONTINUOUS, not staggered: a staggered version with real gaps between tiers was tried first, and a diagonal line from the shallowest spawn (row 19) slipped through a rows-21-23 gap to see the player's nudged spawn, failing all 8 spawnBlockRobust probes for that one enemy. The lesson generalises from the bank-shot search above: a real gap in a spawn's own blocking wall is exactly as dangerous as a new reflecting surface, just for the DIRECT rule instead of the bank one.

The second grey spawns west, in the shadow of arena-04's own mid-field cover block (columns 12-17, rows 24-26) -- geometry that already shipped there as pure decoration (arena-04's notes: cover for the player's left-hand approach, not a spawn blocker) and is reused here as a spawn blocker precisely because it is proven not to open a green ricochet path; only a fresh direct-line check was needed for the new spawn, not a fresh bank-path search.

Cover ratio (open cells no enemy can see from its spawn, walls intact, destructibles excluded): 185 of 1359 = 13.6%, tighter than arena-04's 20.9% and the tightest of all five shipped levels -- the deeper east wall gives its three enemies more combined reach into the board's south half than arena-04's shallower one does. Recomputed by arena-validation.test.ts alongside the other four arenas' figures; arena-04's own notes are corrected to say 'tightest of the four that existed when written' rather than claim a property arena-05 now removes.

claims.why: All seven spawn blocks are solid cells -- the bar's segments for the north three, the continuous east wall for its three, the reused mid-field block for the west grey -- so none opens under a breach. Measured 0 of 28 nudge probes (7 enemies x 4 cardinal offsets) open in either wall phase, including green's ricochet, which is the property three rejected west-wall shapes failed to hold (see notes).

notes: Issue #271: the first board authored FOR versus rather than borrowed from the campaign.
Every wall is placed with its 180-degree partner, so the two halves are the same board turned around: neither player can hold a shape the other cannot.

The maximin spawn policy takes the extreme corners, so the cover that matters is one step INBOARD of them. Each pocket is an L that breaks the corner-to-corner diagonal at its own end while opening onto both edge lanes -- covered on arrival, never one way out.

The centre is a pinwheel of two offset arms plus their partners: you round it clockwise or anticlockwise and neither is shorter, so holding the middle costs a commitment rather than winning by default.
The flank shoulder splits the long way round into an outer edge lane and an inner mid lane, so the two routes between the pockets are different in character rather than mirrored.
The four destructible clusters each plug what would otherwise be the obvious fast line. Breaching one is the tempo decision this map is about, and seeded-destructible variants pre-open a subset.
claims is empty deliberately: lane, sightlineAfterBreach and spawnBlockRobust are campaign-intent vocabulary, and versus boards are validated by versus-catalog-rules.ts instead.

Issue #272 authored this board; issue #424 rebuilt its geometry after human playtesting found that none of the three players could leave their spawn. Named for the arch it forms -- two base corners and one keystone between the pylons at top centre.

THE RULE THIS LAYOUT IS AUTHORED TO, and the reason for the rebuild: a gap does not count as a ROUTE unless a tank fits through it. cellSize is 0.6667 and a tank is 2 x TANK_RADIUS = 1.0 across, so a tank needs 1.5 cells and a one-cell gap has no legal tank-centre position at all. The previous layout's spawns were boxed in by exactly such gaps, which cell-based symmetry, connectivity, path-distance and clearance checks all read as open floor. What this board guarantees is that every spawn has a tank-wide way OUT and that all three share one tank-legal region -- which versus-board.ts's egress gate measures against the real hull, not something this file asserts separately. It is NOT a rule that every gap on the board is tank-wide: narrow gaps are good arena furniture -- cover, notches, firing slits a shell crosses and a hull cannot -- and the gate is safe against them precisely because it refuses to route through them.

STRUCTURE, and why there is so much of it. The first rework of this board passed every gate and read bare, because it had only two horizontal arteries -- everything else was mass, so there was nowhere to put detail without severing a route. This layout is built the other way round: three banded rows of blocks pierced by vertical gaps, offset between bands, so there are many short routes rather than two long ones. 149 solid cells against the bare version's 69. The notches (`#.#` on row 12, `x.x` on row 8) and the rim nubs are deliberately narrower than a tank -- they are cover and firing slits, not routes, and the egress gate is indifferent to them because it refuses to path through anything a hull does not fit. At 27x17 this is close to the ceiling: the board is now the tightest room ratio of any shipped arena at 72.25 open-floor cells per player at N=4, against a bound of 72.

A rectangular grid has no three-fold rotation (its symmetry group has order 4: identity, 180 degrees and two mirrors), so exact rotational equivalence is unavailable at N=3. This board takes the honest substitute the issue's own wording allows -- 'another explicitly justified three-way balance' -- as MIRROR symmetry about column 13. Every wall is placed with its partner at column 26-c, so the two base players hold literally the same shape reflected, and their equivalence is by construction rather than measurement.

The third player is on the mirror axis, so its equivalence to the other two is MEASURED, not constructed. Versus spawns are derived from geometry by pickVersusSpawnCell rather than read from the authored letters, so the claim is about where that policy actually lands: (13,1) between the two pylons, and (1,15) and (25,15) in the base corners -- the same three cells the previous layout placed, now reachable from one another.

TWO DISTANCE METRICS, both stated, because conflating them is what shipped the unplayable board. On the authored CELL metric -- four-neighbour steps over non-wall cells, destructibles blocking -- the three spawns are pairwise 26 apart, an equilateral triangle in path terms. On the TANK-FOOTPRINT lattice that versus-board.ts's egress gate uses, the axis spawn is exactly 17.25 world units from each base and the two bases are 28.333 from each other. The two metrics AGREE that the axis player is equidistant from both bases, and DISAGREE about the base pair: a cell path walks straight through the middle, and a tank must drive around the structure there. That is the arch this board is named for -- the keystone holds the contested middle and the two bases are genuinely far apart -- and it is recorded rather than smoothed, because the previous layout recorded 26/26/26 on the cell metric alone while its three spawns sat in three disconnected tank-legal regions.

The base lane is broken by the jamb at rows 15-16, columns 9-17. It is there for CONCEALMENT: without it the two base spawns see each other straight down row 15, and allPairsConcealed fails. It is two rows deep rather than three so that the corridor above it stays clear enough to drive, which is what keeps the detour drivable instead of merely walkable.

Four destructible clusters, every one mirrored about column 13: the cheeks of the notch on row 8, the outer block faces on row 9, the central cap on row 10, and the lower block faces on row 13. 19 cells in all. Breaching one is the tempo decision, and seeded-destructible variants pre-open a subset. Two constraints shape where they can go. Destructible cells count as TRAVERSABLE in pickVersusSpawnCell's geodesic graph, so their placement moves the spawn picks and several otherwise-reasonable clusters were rejected during authoring for shifting the maximin set off the three cells above. And none of them caps a spawn pocket: sealedSpawns is 0 at N=2, 3 and 4, so every player reaches the shared floor without firing a shot. The set that ships is swept at removal fraction 0.4 over seeds 1..10 and holds the spawn set, concealment and the egress gate on every draw.

The authored P and B letters serve the campaign-facing loadArena path and resolution.test.ts's grid rule (every authored spawn coordinate must be odd in world space, i.e. an index congruent to 1 mod 3); they are NOT the versus spawns and deliberately sit away from the three the policy picks.
claims is empty deliberately, same as vs-duel-01: lane, sightlineAfterBreach and spawnBlockRobust are campaign-intent vocabulary, and versus boards are validated by versus-catalog-rules.ts instead.
Issue #273: the first board authored for FOUR players. Named for the four mirror-equal quarters it divides into, one per spawn.

Where the three-player board had to settle for a measured equivalence, four players fit a rectangle's symmetry group exactly. Every solid wall is placed with a partner at column 26-c AND at row 16-r, so the board is invariant under both mirrors and therefore under the 180-degree rotation they compose. The four spawns pickVersusSpawnCell lands on -- (1,1), (25,1), (1,15) and (25,15) -- are a single orbit of that group, so their equivalence is by construction, not by measurement.

What that buys, measured on the authored grid with solid AND destructible cells blocking -- the board before anything is breached, which is the convention versus-catalog-rules.ts uses: every spawn's three path distances to the others are the same multiset, {30, 32, 38} -- 30 to its vertical neighbour, 32 to its horizontal one, 38 to the corner diagonally opposite. Reachable cells within eight steps are 37 for all four. Remove every destructible and the sets relax together to {26, 30, 38} and 42 reachable, still identical across the four. Equal-for-all in both states is the claim: a board that is fair only while its cover stands is not a fair board.

The two edge distances differ because 27x17 is not square, and no wall placement can equalise them: the horizontal separation is 24 columns and the vertical 14 rows, so the lanes that join them cannot be made the same length without breaking the mirror that makes the four spawns equivalent in the first place. Equal-for-all was preferred over equal-to-each-other. Which of the two is longer is not even fixed -- the cross-lane destructibles put the horizontal hop above the vertical on the authored board (32 against 30) and below it once breached (26 against 30) -- which is why the claim is about the multiset rather than about any one edge.

The rim blocks at rows 7-9, columns 0-3 and 23-26 are what make the corners the maximin picker's own choice rather than an authored wish. Without them the open outer column joins two vertically adjacent corners cheaply, the picker prefers a mid-row cell to the corner, and the four spawns come out as (1,1), (19,1), (7,15) and (25,15) -- measured on the rim-less draft. That set is 180-degree symmetric and nothing more: two orbits of two rather than one orbit of four, so the two mid-row players hold a different shape from the two corner ones. Blocking the outer lanes lengthens every corner-to-corner edge path past the best interior alternative, and the corners win on their own merits.

Teams is declared as well as FFA, and the split is a property of the geometry rather than a hope: teamOf(slot) = slot % 2 over the picker's order puts (1,1) and (25,1) on team 0 and (1,15) and (25,15) on team 1 -- the top pair against the bottom pair. The board is mirror-symmetric about row 8, so the two teams hold reflected territory, and teammates start the same distance apart on both sides: 32 authored, 26 breached. The pairing could as easily have come out diagonal, which would still be 2v2 and still pass every geometry validator while handing one team both 38-step corners, so it is asserted rather than assumed.

Twenty destructible cells in mirrored clusters: the pair flanking the core on rows 4 and 12, the four on the open cross-lanes at rows 2 and 14, and the pair on the mid lane at rows 7 and 9. Each plugs a line that would otherwise run clear, so breaching one is a tempo decision; seeded-destructible variants pre-open a subset, and the pinned seed sweep validates that the six spawn pairs stay concealed through it.

The authored P and B letters serve the campaign-facing loadArena path and resolution.test.ts's grid rule (an index congruent to 1 mod 3 in both axes); they sit on the mirror axis at column 13 and are NOT the versus spawns.

Normal-speed playtest, both declared modes, through the real scripted-player AI at the real 60 Hz for 90 seconds (quad-playtest.measure.test.ts, seeds 7/11/23). FFA: first contact at 3.45-4.33 s, first kill at 6.52-12.05 s, 6-9 kills and 2-4 breaches per match. Teams: identical first contact to the tick, and ZERO kills in all three seeds against 45-49 mines laid, versus 15-21 mines for 6-9 kills in FFA. That contrast is the finding and it is a property of the mode rather than of this board -- the scripted AI fights almost entirely with mines here (0 shells fired in all six matches), and with friendly fire off a mine cannot harm the layer's partner, so a 2v2 halves the population of mines that can kill any given tank. Recorded rather than tuned around: nothing about the geometry changes between the two modes, and loadArena places all four players identically in both.
